title: Kinetic competition controls loss-induced exceptional points of Hubbard pairs
abstract: Two-body loss can bind two fermions in a Hubbard lattice, yet the binding threshold in the infinite lattice need not be an exceptional point (EP). At fixed total momentum $\mathbf{K}$, the hops of the two particles interfere into a relative-motion hopping along each lattice direction, which sets the kinetic energy of the relative motion. On a hypercubic lattice, the threshold $g_c=1/[πρ_2(0)]$ is an EP precisely when the maximum kinetic energy along one direction exceeds the sum of the transverse maxima. This dominance keeps every transverse-momentum scattering channel propagating near the band center, making the local pair Green function purely imaginary there. Two real-energy scattering zeros associated with coherent perfect absorption then coalesce at the threshold into a second-order EP of the analytically continued pair problem, where loss restores the parity-time symmetry of the pair's scattering solutions. Without a dominant direction, binding occurs without coalescence and without breaking of that symmetry. Total momentum can therefore select EP sectors even on isotropic lattices. More broadly, the kinetic structure of the two-particle continuum determines whether loss-induced binding and exceptional degeneracy coincide.
summary: This theoretical study examines how two-body loss induces binding in Hubbard pairs, determining when this binding threshold coincides with an Exceptional Point (EP). The key finding is that the kinetic structure of the pair's relative motion dictates whether this EP occurs, showing that momentum selection can stabilize EP behavior even on highly symmetric lattices.
main_problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which the binding threshold for a two-fermion pair, induced by two-body loss, coincides with an Exceptional Point (EP) in the analytically continued pair problem.
main_result: The occurrence of an EP is critically controlled by the kinetic structure of the relative motion; dominance in one direction can select EP sectors even on isotropic lattices, while isotropic lattices may exhibit binding without EP coalescence.
method: The analysis uses the no-jump framework, analyzing the secular equation derived from the Green's function, and comparing results from the resolvent route with the Bethe ansatz in 1D.
model_or_system: The system is a two-fermion pair in a Hubbard lattice subjected to a two-body loss term (imaginary on-site interaction). The dynamics are analyzed by treating the relative motion of the pair.
key_observables: Binding threshold ($g_c$), Exceptional Point (EP) condition, pair density of states ($ho_2(0)$), and the nature of the transition (PT breaking/restoration).
important_parameters: Loss rate ($g$), total momentum ($\mathbf{K}$), and the relative hopping structure (kinetic competition).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a purely dissipative on-site interaction and relies on approximations like the no-jump dynamics and the continuum limit for the Green's function.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relative motion energy spectrum, the transition between PT breaking and restoration across different dimensions (1D, 2D, 3D), and how total momentum selects the EP.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the general condition for EP coincidence, analyzing the role of kinetic competition across different lattice dimensions, and providing detailed mathematical confirmations using the resolvent route and the Bethe ansatz for the 1D case.
why_interesting: This work connects concepts from open quantum systems (loss, EPs) directly to strongly correlated electron physics (Hubbard model), providing a detailed mechanism for how particle loss can induce non-Hermitian degeneracies that are sensitive to lattice geometry and momentum.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Loss-induced binding as scattering of the relative motion. (a) At total momentum K the relative coordinate r = r↑−r↓advances by ei when the up fermion hops forward or the down fermion backward; the amplitudes interfere to 2ti cos(Ki/2), whose magnitude is the relative hopping Ji, and the loss is one absorbing site, −ig, at r = 0. (b)–(d) At fixed ky the motion along x is a channel of half-width 2Jx shifted by −2Jy cos ky, open (light blue) or closed (grey) at energy E. An EP needs a window in which every channel is open (green), |E| < 2(Jx −Jy): (b) Jy = 0, the whole band; (c) Jy = Jx/2; (d) Jy = Jx, the window closes and there is no EP.

FIG. 2. PT breaking and restoration of one pair at K = 0 on the chain, the square lattice at ty = tx/2 and the cubic lattice at ty = tz = tx/4: (a) Re E and (b) Im E against g/tx. Curves, L →∞: the two CPA zeros below the critical interaction (dashed verticals) and the bound pair above it. Circles: the two most-decaying eigenvalues of finite lattices; above the critical interaction the second one, which stays just below Im E = 0, is drawn in (b) only.

FIG. 3. The threshold from one dimension to three, at K = 0. (a) gc against the summed transverse hopping, in two dimensions [Eq. (4), black] and in three with ty = tz [Eq. (5), red]; dotted, the one-dimensional value. Stars mark ty + tz = tx, where the window closes: gc vanishes in two dimensions and stays finite in three. (b) ρ2(E), solid in two dimensions, dashed in three: the saddle reaching the band center makes ρ2(0) diverge in two dimensions but is only a kink in three.

FIG. 4. Total momentum switches the pair EP. (a) Square lattice: gc in every sector K; the threshold is an EP except on the diagonals |Kx| = |Ky| (dashed), where gc = 0. (b) gc along Γ–X–M–Γ, with X = (π, 0) and M = (π, π); solid, EP; dashed, no EP. (c) Cubic lattice in the plane Kx = 0, with X = (0, 0, π) and M = (0, π, π): gc in the EP sectors, white elsewhere; color scale as in (a). (d) Cubic lattice along Γ–X– M–R–Γ, with X = (π, 0, 0), M = (π, π, 0) and R = (π, π, π); line styles as in (b).
